name: Beard vitamins (zinc, B-complex, D)

card.summary: Multivitamin-style stacks of zinc, B vitamins and vitamin D aimed at beard growth; deficiencies can affect hair, but no trials show extra vitamins thicken a beard.
card.note: Biotin can interfere with some lab tests; high vitamin D intake can be toxic.

quick.overview:
Some beard-growth routines include over-the-counter zinc, B-complex (often biotin) and vitamin D, on the idea that nutrient shortfalls limit facial hair.

Reference sources link deficiencies of some of these nutrients to hair thinning, but no clinical trials were found testing them for beard growth in people who are not deficient.
quick.mechanism: Zinc, biotin and other B vitamins are involved in skin and hair biology, and deficiency states are associated with hair changes. Whether supplementing beyond adequate intake changes beard growth has not been studied.
quick.risks: Biotin at 5 mg/day or more can distort thyroid and vitamin D lab results. Vitamin D toxicity, with high blood calcium, can occur at very high doses. Supplements in the US are not approved for effectiveness before sale.

lead: Beard-growth stacks sold or discussed online often combine zinc, B-complex vitamins (frequently biotin) and vitamin D. People take them hoping for a fuller, thicker beard: the reasoning is that hair follicles need adequate nutrients, so correcting a shortfall could let facial hair grow closer to its genetic potential, while some stack vitamin D with K2 as part of general optimisation.[1][2][6]

Deficiencies of some of these nutrients are associated with hair changes: zinc deficiency with thin, sparse hair, and biotin deficiency, which is rare, with hair thinning.[1][2] Reference sources report that there are no randomized controlled trials proving biotin supplementation helps healthy people's hair, and general hair-loss references state that dietary supplements are not typically recommended outside deficiency.[1][4]

No studies found address these vitamins specifically for beard growth. Beard density and pattern are driven largely by genetics and androgen sensitivity, so most beard discussion focuses on those, with vitamins treated as a supporting measure.[4][12]

paras: Wikipedia's beard article says growth rate is genetic and linked to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) stimulating follicles in the beard area; DHT is made from testosterone, whose levels vary with season, and beards develop during puberty with DHT continuing to influence growth afterwards.[12] This is the context in which vitamin routines are framed: as supporting general hair and skin health around a trait that is largely set by genetics and hormones, not as a replacement for them.[12][4]

Zinc deficiency is described as causing alopecia ("thin and sparse hair"), skin problems and impaired taste or smell.[2] Zinc is a cofactor in many enzymes, which is the basis for its inclusion in hair and beard stacks.

Wikipedia lists thin, sparse hair, acne, eczema, dry scaling skin and seborrheic dermatitis among signs of zinc deficiency, along with impaired wound healing, reduced taste and smell in severe cases, and lower testosterone with delayed puberty.[2] It names diets high in phytate-rich whole grains, malabsorption, heavy alcohol use, intense exercise, bariatric surgery and chronic disease among causes, and oysters, meat, beans, nuts and dark chicken meat among food sources.[2] The article does not give treatment doses or discuss excess zinc.[2]

Biotin deficiency is rare in people eating a normal diet, and mild cases can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or a facial rash; most cases arise from a genetic condition, biotinidase deficiency.[1] Biotin is the B vitamin most associated with hair, and B-complex products bundle it with other B vitamins. Iron and vitamin B12 deficiencies are listed among less common causes of hair loss.[4]

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin made in skin from sunlight and obtained from diet and supplements.[3] Looksmaxxing forum users discuss vitamin D, often alongside K2, as part of general health optimisation, with some checking blood levels in winter.[6][7]

sections.h: History of biotin and the hair link
paras: Biotin's connection to hair goes back to nutrition experiments in the early twentieth century. In 1916 W. G. Bateman linked raw egg white in the diet to toxic symptoms, and in 1927 Margarete Boas and Helen Parsons described "egg-white injury" in rats, which included hair loss and dermatitis.[1]

Paul Gyorgy investigated the protective factor from 1933 and in 1939 named it "Vitamin H" (from the German words for skin and hair); by 1940 several independently isolated compounds were recognised as the same molecule and named biotin. In 1941 Gyorgy showed egg-white injury results from avidin in raw egg white binding biotin.[1] This history is part of why biotin became the vitamin most associated with hair and why B-complex beard products emphasise it.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and beard-growth routines
paras: Beard-growth routines commonly pair supplements with minoxidil, dermarolling, grooming products and sleep or training advice. On looksmax.org, a poster says biotin is still useful for hair even though another thread member says it does not affect water retention, while other threads discuss vitamin D and K2 and winter vitamin D testing.[6][7][8][9] Posters' amounts vary widely and are not recommendations on this wiki.

Biotin supplements of 5 mg/day or more can interfere with immunoassays used for thyroid hormones and vitamin D levels, giving falsely normal or abnormal results; a 2017 FDA safety communication on this is cited.[1] Vitamin D toxicity is rare but occurs with high-dose supplements, causing high blood calcium; the US tolerable upper intake for adults is 4,000 IU/day.[3]
Multivitamin and mineral products may supply zinc as gluconate, sulfate or acetate, and Wikipedia notes it is unclear which form works best.[2]

The FDA safety communication on biotin lab interference was issued on 28 November 2017; Wikipedia reports that clinicians may advise stopping biotin for 48 hours or longer before testing, depending on the test and dose, and that US newborn screening for biotinidase deficiency began in 1984.[1]
In the US supplements are not required to be approved for effectiveness before sale, and labels may carry structure/function claims with a disclaimer that the FDA has not evaluated them.[1]

No studies found for beard growth. Related general information: a review cited by Wikipedia found no randomized trials showing biotin supplementation helps hair in healthy people.[1] Trials of B vitamins in healthy people have looked at other outcomes: a 2023 randomized double-blind crossover trial in 32 healthy adults tested 28 days of a B1/B2/B6/B12 supplement against placebo for fatigue and exercise performance, and a 2021 meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials with 6,276 participants found no effect of B12 or B-complex on cognition or depression in people without overt deficiency.[10][11]

Beard supplements are sold as dedicated 'beard growth vitamins' and as general multivitamins. Beard care in general has grown with the wider acceptance of facial hair, which Wikipedia notes in connection with the popularity of beard oils and grooming products.[5]

lore.intro: Vitamins are a common, low-cost first step in beard and hair discussion on looksmax.org and similar forums.[7][8][9]

claims.claim: Biotin supports healthy hair and beard growth
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says it is useful to take biotin for healthy hair and hair growth.[8]
claims.experts: Biotin deficiency is rare and can cause hair thinning; reference sources report no randomized trials showing biotin helps hair in healthy people.[1]

claims.claim: Vitamin D deficiency can hold back appearance and testosterone-related traits
claims.believers: Looksmax.org threads urge members to check vitamin D levels, discuss how much deficiency 'is holding me back', and cover D3 with K2.[7][9]
claims.experts: Vitamin D toxicity occurs at high doses and the US upper intake for adults is 4,000 IU/day.[3] No studies found test vitamin D for beard growth.

claims.claim: Zinc is needed for thick facial hair
claims.believers: Stacks include zinc on the reasoning that deficiency thins hair.[2]
claims.experts: Zinc deficiency is associated with thin, sparse hair; benefit beyond correcting deficiency has not been studied for beards.[2]

chain: Supplements correct possible zinc, biotin or vitamin D shortfalls
Follicles and skin have the nutrients they use for hair growth
angle.text: Users add zinc, a B-complex with biotin and vitamin D to their daily routine to support beard growth and the skin under the beard. The expected benefit is strongest where a deficiency exists; effects in people with adequate intake are claimed rather than measured.
